summary:
MARS EXPLORER is a proposed geographic information platform designed to support the planning of human expeditions on Mars. We developed a conceptual design for a demonstration prototype focused on Jezero Crater. It proposes integrating scientific information from multiple NASA missions through map layers showing topography, orbital imagery, geology, and previous exploration activities.

The project addresses the challenge of bringing together scattered datasets and making them easier to interpret, helping explorers understand the terrain and identify areas of scientific interest. It proposes comparing three route alternatives: the shortest distance, the lowest topographic difficulty, and the greatest scientific interest, using existing visualization and analysis tools. At this stage, the routes are illustrative and have not yet been calculated or validated.

The project’s importance lies in using decades of robotic exploration data to support informed decisions and contribute to more efficient and safer planning for future human expeditions.
details:
MARS EXPLORER is a proposed geographic information platform designed to support the planning of future human expeditions on Mars. Our team developed a conceptual design for a demonstration prototype focused on Jezero Crater, a region explored by NASA’s Perseverance rover.

How it works

The proposed platform brings scientific information from multiple NASA missions into a shared mapping environment. Its layers would include topography and elevation, high-resolution orbital imagery, geological and mineralogical characteristics, slopes and potential obstacles, points of scientific interest, and previous exploration activities.

The workflow begins with collecting and organizing relevant datasets, checking their coverage and compatibility, and displaying them as map layers. Users would then examine the terrain, select a starting point and destination, and compare three exploration priorities:

  • Shortest distance: prioritize a more direct route between selected locations.
  • Lowest topographic difficulty: prioritize terrain with gentler slopes and fewer identified obstacles.
  • Greatest scientific interest: prioritize access to locations relevant to scientific investigation.

The current presentation includes illustrative route overlays to explain these alternatives. These routes have not been calculated or validated, and the project does not yet provide an operational navigation system.

Benefits and intended impact

MARS EXPLORER aims to make information from different missions easier to access, interpret, and compare. Viewing terrain characteristics alongside scientific targets could help users understand the trade-offs between travel distance, topographic difficulty, and exploration objectives.

The intended impact is to demonstrate how decades of robotic exploration data can support informed planning for future human missions. The project could also serve as an educational resource for students interested in planetary science, geographic information systems, and space exploration. Improvements in expedition efficiency or safety remain expected benefits that would require further testing.

Scientific sources and development tools

The proposed scientific inputs include MRO HiRISE and CTX imagery, MGS MOLA topography, available Mars Odyssey thermal and mineralogical information, and Perseverance photographs, geological observations, and traverses. NASA’s Planetary Data System provides access to archived mission data.

For this stage, we prepared an editable presentation using published NASA imagery and conceptual diagrams. The planned demonstration workflow uses NASA Mars Trek for map visualization, Google Sheets for organizing and comparing information, Google Drive for file distribution, and Canva for visual design. QGIS is an optional tool for geographic analysis. Integration of these tools has not yet been completed or verified.

The proposed demonstrator does not require custom programming or specialized hardware. It is intended to use existing software on a standard computer with internet access.

Creative approach

The project’s creative contribution is its proposed combination of layered scientific information with three clearly differentiated exploration priorities. Rather than assuming one route meets every objective, the concept makes the trade-offs visible and connects geographic analysis with scientific investigation.

Factors considered by the team

Our team considered data availability, spatial resolution, geographic coverage, coordinate-system compatibility, source traceability, and ease of interpretation. We also considered the limitations of regional elevation data for assessing local slopes and obstacles.

We distinguish between real scientific imagery, proposed functions, and hypothetical routes. Lower topographic difficulty alone does not establish that a route is safe for astronauts. Operational planning would require additional assessment of environmental conditions, communications, equipment, and human constraints.

The initial focus on Jezero keeps the project manageable while allowing future expansion to other Martian regions and additional scientific datasets.
